The Christianity that took shape in the West during the Boomer and Gen X generations produced something remarkable: churches that resembled the society they were supposed to transform.

The second half of the twentieth century saw the rise of televangelists, megachurches, celebrity pastors, political Christianity, and a religious culture concerned with personal fulfillment.

Much of this was inherited from earlier movements. But the Boomer era brought these tendencies into the age of television, mass consumerism, and modern identity politics.

The consequences are still with us.

Here are five reasons this expression of Christianity has done so much damage.

1. Christianity Became Therapy

Somewhere along the way, Christianity became concerned with making people feel good about themselves.

Repentance became personal healing. Sin became emotional baggage. Salvation was presented as the beginning of a happier, more successful life.

The language changed because the priorities changed.

Christ commanded His followers to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow Him (Luke 9:23). Modern therapeutic Christianity offers a more comfortable arrangement: come as you are, feel accepted, and leave encouraged.

There is nothing wrong with comfort. Scripture offers plenty of it. But comfort without correction produces Christians who expect God to affirm their desires rather than transform their character.

A faith that cannot confront a man’s sins cannot save him from them.

2. Christianity Became a Political Identity

Western Christians learned to identify themselves through political movements.

On the right, Christianity became entangled with nationalism, electoral loyalty, and the defense of a particular vision of Western civilization.

On the left, Christianity became interpreted through progressive social movements and their changing moral priorities.

Both tendencies created the same problem.

Instead of judging political movements according to Scripture, Christians began judging Scripture according to their political commitments.

The result is a religious culture where political agreement can matter more than obedience to Christ.

Christians are called to exercise judgment in public life. But the Kingdom of God cannot be reduced to a voting bloc, a national identity, or a political platform.

When politics becomes the foundation of Christian identity, faith becomes another instrument in the struggle for earthly power.

3. The Church Became a Business

The modern Western church learned the language of the marketplace remarkably well.

Pastors became celebrities. Sermons became products. Worship became entertainment. Congregations became audiences whose attention had to be captured and retained.

The megachurch model brought this mentality into full view.

Attendance, revenue, branding, production quality, and personal influence became measures of religious success.

And when the congregation becomes the customer, the temptation is obvious: give people what keeps them coming back.

Difficult teachings become inconvenient. Correction threatens retention. Entertainment becomes easier than discipleship.

Paul warned Timothy that people would gather teachers according to their own desires, seeking what their ears wanted to hear (2 Timothy 4:3–4).

A church can fill thousands of seats and still fail to produce mature Christians.

4. Christianity Learned to Obey Modern Culture

Every generation faces pressure to accommodate the moral expectations of its society.

Modern Western Christianity responded by adjusting its teachings to fit those expectations.

The sexual revolution transformed public attitudes toward marriage, sexuality, family, and personal autonomy. Churches were forced to confront these changes, and many responded by reconsidering convictions that Christians had inherited for centuries.

The underlying problem reaches beyond sexual ethics.

Modern society treats individual desire as a source of moral authority. Christianity teaches that human desires themselves require examination, discipline, and sometimes rejection.

Those two positions cannot be reconciled.

Yet much of modern Christianity has tried to make them compatible by reducing obedience to personal sincerity and treating moral boundaries as obstacles to individual fulfillment.

“Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” (Romans 12:2)

A Christianity that adjusts itself to the prevailing culture eventually loses the ability to challenge that culture.

5. Western Christians Forgot How Old Christianity Is

Perhaps the strangest consequence of modern Western Christianity is how little many Christians know about their own religious history.

Entire generations have grown up knowing contemporary pastors, denominational arguments, and modern theological systems while remaining unfamiliar with the ancient Christian world.

Christianity existed in Ethiopia, Egypt, Syria, Armenia, and across the eastern Mediterranean long before the modern Western denominations appeared.

These communities preserved ancient liturgies, manuscripts, theological traditions, and ways of Christian life that developed across centuries.

Yet many Western Christians approach Christianity as though its history revolves entirely around Rome, the Protestant Reformation, and the religious movements that followed.

Some even mistake the practices and assumptions of their own denomination for Christianity itself.

This historical amnesia has consequences.

When Christians lose contact with their ancient inheritance, they become more vulnerable to treating recent innovations as timeless truths.

A religious culture that barely remembers its past will struggle to recognize when it has departed from it.

What Remains?

Look at what these five developments have in common.

Therapeutic Christianity places personal comfort at the center. Political Christianity places earthly allegiance there. Consumer Christianity answers to market demand. Cultural accommodation answers to modern society. Historical amnesia leaves Christians unable to recognize how recently many of their assumptions developed.

In each case, something else begins exercising authority over Christian life.

The problem goes deeper than declining church attendance or the disappearance of Christian influence from public institutions.

What good is preserving Christian influence if the Christianity being preserved has already surrendered much of its character?

The West does not need another religious marketing campaign, another celebrity pastor, or another political movement wearing the cross.

It needs Christians who remember whom they follow, what He commanded, and what obedience requires.

That would be a far more meaningful revival than filling the pews.
